title: The ones who carry it
hookLine: millions have memorized the whole Qur'an, many as children

lines: A BOY OF ELEVEN STANDS UP.
cards: In a small room in Cairo, or Kano, or Karachi, or a converted storefront in Minneapolis, a boy of eleven stands before his teacher and a row of family. He recites.
Not a surah: the whole Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, from memory, for hours, while the teacher follows along and listens for a single slip. When he finishes, his mother is crying.
There's a word for what he has become.

teach.h: HAFIZ: ONE WHO GUARDS AND KEEPS
teach.b: The word is hafiz; for a woman, hafizah. It comes from a root meaning to guard, to preserve, to keep, and that root is in the Qur'an itself.
In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian." Guardian there comes from the same root.

teach.h: KEPT IN PEOPLE, OFTEN FROM CHILDHOOD
teach.b: In the tradition, the memorizers are part of how that guarding happens: the book is kept not only on paper but in people. Nobody keeps a count of them.
Often they begin as children, in schools built for exactly this, a few lines at a time, reciting each day's new portion to a teacher and revising the old.

The Qur'an seems made for it; its rhythm and rhyme hold together in the memory. It says of itself, in Pickthall: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?"
The Prophet ﷺ spoke about those who carry it.
A hadith says the one who recites skillfully will be with the noble, righteous scribes, the angels; and the one who recites with difficulty, stumbling over it, gets a double reward.
Stumbling, and still going, counts twice. The title even reached poetry: tradition says the Persian poet Hafez of Shiraz took his name because he knew the Qur'an by heart.
And it isn't finished when the last surah is learned. Keeping it is its own work.

teach.h: TEND IT, LIKE A HOBBLED CAMEL
teach.b: The Prophet compared it to a hobbled camel: tend it, or it slips away.

how: Many Muslim children and adults memorize the Qur'an in dedicated schools and circles, reciting a new portion to a teacher each day and revising what they know; a hafiz often leads the long Ramadan night prayers.

o: a guard who keeps watch over a mosque
one who keeps the whole Qur'an by heart
a scholar who explains the Qur'an's verses

s: only scholars memorize the whole Qur'an
hafiz is a title for anyone who keeps the whole Qur'an by heart, and many start as children.
the one who stumbles while reciting gets a double reward
the one who recites with difficulty has two rewards.
the Prophet compared it to a hobbled camel: tend it, or it slips away.

games.q: you're reciting and keep stumbling over the words. what does the hadith say about you?
o: stop until you can do it perfectly.
games.why: the one who recites with difficulty gets a double reward. stumbling, and still going, counts twice.

practice: Choose one short verse you don't know yet: the second line of al-Ikhlas, Allahus-samad, is a gentle start, or any short line you'd like to keep.

Say it five times slowly while looking at it, then five times with your eyes closed, and if you stumble, it counts. If you're here to learn about the path rather than to practice it, learn the verse's meaning by heart instead.

wordCard.voice: Hafiz. One who has memorized the whole Qur'an: literally a guardian, a keeper. For a woman, hafizah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a guardian, a keeper; one who has memorized the whole Qur'an. for a woman, hafizah.

carryVoice: Your line: carried by heart. One verse, kept and tended, is a real beginning. See you tomorrow.
